# Exact root-dependent tree optimization on cactus graphs

Problem: TOP-30003996  
Claim type: Partial result  
Author: /root/hundred_algorithms

**Exact scope.** For a connected cactus graph with arbitrary explicitly encoded rational root-dependent directed arc costs, the literal objective Σr c_r(T^r) is exactly minimized by independent bridge/cycle-block optimization. A cycle of length ℓ needs O(nℓ²) rational additions; total bit time is polynomial in the full cost-table length. This is a tractable graph subclass, not a repeated general hardness proof.

The earlier manuscript already proves the requested general NP-hardness through a SAT reduction. Here we keep the same root-dependent objective and both possible orientation conventions, and identify a broad exactly solvable subclass. A cactus is a graph in which each edge belongs to at most one simple cycle. Its blocks are bridges and simple cycles, meeting at articulation vertices in a block-cut tree.

Every spanning tree contains every bridge. In each cycle block it deletes exactly one edge, and choices in different blocks are independent. Indeed connectivity requires connecting all vertices of each block through that block, because the block-cut incidence graph is a tree; an intact cycle would violate acyclicity, while deleting two edges from one cycle would disconnect it. Conversely deleting one edge from each cycle and retaining bridges gives a connected acyclic spanning graph.

For each block B and global root r, let a(B,r) be r itself if r belongs to B; otherwise let it be the unique articulation of B encountered on the route from r through the block-cut tree. This projection depends only on the graph, not on the deleted cycle edges. In every spanning tree, the orientation of its edges inside B away from r is exactly the orientation of the local block tree away from a(B,r). The path first reaches B through that articulation; rerouting paths in other blocks cannot change it.

Thus, for local choice T_B,
\[
 \sum_r c_r(T^r)=\sum_B F_B(T_B),\qquad
 F_B(T_B)=\sum_r\sum_{a\in T_B^{a(B,r)}}c_r(a).
\]
The feasible choices form a Cartesian product over the blocks, so the minimum of the sum is the sum of the independent local minima. This does not require nonnegative costs: each local feasible family is finite and every global combination is a spanning tree.

For a bridge its unique edge is forced, with its orientation evaluated separately for each root. For a cycle with ℓ edges, enumerate its ℓ possible deleted edges. For each candidate and each root, traverse the resulting path tree from a(B,r), summing its ℓ−1 directed arc costs. This costs O(nℓ²) rational additions over all candidates. Keep a minimizing deletion, breaking ties deterministically. The union of these local choices is the desired global optimal tree.

A simple depth-first traversal finds the bridge/cycle blocks and verifies the cactus promise; a noncactus input is rejected as outside the scope. Computing all root projections can be done by traversing the block-cut tree once per root. A conservative arithmetic-operation count is O(n(m+ΣB cycle |B|²)), plus input reading. Each objective adds at most nm entries from the explicit input table. If its total binary length is L, the product of all input denominators has at most L bits, so exact rational comparisons and sums have polynomial bit length in L+log(nm+2). Hence the overall bit complexity is polynomial in L, n and m; no unit-cost real oracle is used. Output size O(nlog(n+2)) is included. Common-denominator arithmetic is one explicit conservative implementation.

For an inward-root convention, reverse every directed arc in the supplied cost table before applying the proof. The numerical correspondence is exact. The one-vertex graph has no blocks and optimum zero; a tree has only forced blocks and its unique spanning tree is returned. Negative rational costs, parallel choices with equal optimum and roots at articulations are all covered.

The algorithm does not extend merely because a graph has small average degree. Its essential property is the unique block-entry articulation and the independent one-deletion choices within cycle blocks. In a noncactus biconnected block, spanning-tree choices can alter multiple root paths jointly; that is where the present factorization ceases to apply.
